title: Research
text:
I apply control theory to complex network systems, focusing on decentralised performance and stability analysis for systems that require plug-and-play functionality.
My primary application is AC power grids. As synchronous generation is replaced by inverter-based resources, the rotational inertia of the grid is disappearing, and the distributed nature of the evolving system means classical small-signal techniques — such as eigenvalue analysis on a fixed, monolithic, system-wide model — are no longer scalable or appropriate. The same decentralised techniques carry over to distributed optimisation, where decentralised algorithms are used to control physical networks.

title: Research
text:
Themes

Theme 01

Decentralised stability conditions for AC grids
I develop decentralised small-signal stability certificates for AC grids in the frequency-domain. These take the form of quadratic constraints imposed on individual subsystems — devices, buses and lines — which collectively ensure the full interconnection is stable. A companion work shows that grid subsystem representations exhibit inherent unstable open-loop poles in many common network configurations, even when the aggregate interconnection is stable and well behaved, making decentralised analysis more difficult. The proposed stability framework accounts for such complexities encountered in real system models.

In practice. These conditions are the foundation for a grid code: a connection standard a device manufacturer can test or design against without needing to know the details of the full network. Because each certificate is local, adding, re-rating or removing plant does not trigger a system-wide restudy, and device controllers do not need re-tuning every time the topology changes.

Related: Part I and Part II of the plug-and-play stability conditions; unstable poles in subsystem representations.



Theme 02

Optimality in decentralised and distributed systems
Decentralised control design gives stability and scalability, but says little about how well the network performs as a whole. Performance is crucial in many network applications, such as power systems and internet congestion control. I use inverse optimal control to link stability and performance, showing that under appropriate local conditions, decentralised passive controllers are exactly the solution of a network-wide optimal control problem. This argument extends to distributed optimisation algorithms, viewed as dynamical systems: a broad class of augmented primal–dual methods prove optimal for a cost penalising deviations from optimality during the transient.

In practice. Both results give a performance metric where there were previously only stability guarantees and simulation studies, showing what a controller’s or an algorithm’s parameters actually trade off. Synthesis for linear systems reduces to an LMI — a solver call rather than hand-tuning.

Related: inverse optimal control for passive network systems (IEEE TAC); passivity-based design for converter-based microgrids; an optimal control interpretation of augmented distributed optimisation algorithms (under review, Automatica) and its conference version.
